lines.text: This tiny square of metal and silicon... is the brain of your computer.
Every click, every game, every video you watch, all of it runs through here.
It lives right in the middle of the motherboard, locked into a socket.
And a cooler sits on top, so it doesn't cook itself.
So let's take it apart.
On top, the heat spreader. A metal lid that pulls heat away from the chip.
Underneath, the real star. A thin sliver of silicon, called the die.
And at the bottom, the substrate, with over a thousand tiny contacts that connect it to the rest of your PC.
Now zoom into the die.
These blocks are cores. Each one is its own mini brain, and most CPUs today have somewhere between six and sixteen of them, all working at the same time.
Right next to them is the cache. Super fast memory that keeps whatever the cores need right now, within arm's reach.
But go deeper. And deeper.
Down here, everything is made of transistors. Billions of microscopic switches.
On. Off. On. Off.
Each one is just a one, or a zero. But flip billions of them, billions of times every second, and you get... everything.
Think of it like a kitchen.
The cores are the chefs. The cache is the counter right beside them.
And clock speed, measured in gigahertz, is how fast each chef works. Five gigahertz means five billion steps, every single second.
So when you're picking one, watch two numbers.
More cores, for multitasking, streaming and editing.
Higher clock speed, for snappy, smooth gaming.
Get that balance right, and your whole computer feels instant.
